recent_posts.title: How Plausible built a profitable startup by ignoring standard startup advice
recent_posts.summary: Plausible Analytics shares how they built a profitable, independent analytics company over seven years by rejecting conventional startup wisdom. Key principles: stay self-funded to force product-market clarity, keep the team small (10 people), charge from day one with a subscription model, rely on organic growth instead of paid ads or aggressive funnels, and prioritize survival over breakout growth. The result is slow but compounding progress — profitable within a few years, no investor pressure, and still enjoying the work after seven years.

recent_posts.title: How to manage Plausible Analytics across multiple client sites with Google Tag Manager
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide for agencies and freelancers managing Plausible Analytics across multiple client sites using Google Tag Manager. Covers setting up the official Plausible GTM template, creating per-client containers, enabling enhanced measurements (outbound links, file downloads, form submissions, 404 tracking), adding custom event tracking without code changes, and best practices for multi-container management. Also touches on localhost/staging exclusions, GTM limitations for server-side events, and extending reporting with Looker Studio.

recent_posts.title: Attribution Modeling: What it is and How to do it with Plausible Analytics
recent_posts.summary: Attribution modeling assigns credit to marketing touchpoints that lead to conversions. Traditional approaches are becoming less reliable due to cookie restrictions and ad blockers. Plausible Analytics offers a privacy-first, cookieless alternative that provides real (non-modeled) data. A practical framework is outlined using four layers: last-touch attribution via the Sources report, first-touch approximation via Entry pages, campaign-level attribution via UTM parameters, and funnel analysis for behavioral context. This approach suits small-to-mid-size SaaS and B2B teams that don't need complex multi-touch modeling.

recent_posts.title: Handpicked list of privacy-focused European alternatives to big tech products for B2B [Updated]
recent_posts.summary: A curated list of 18 privacy-focused, GDPR-compliant European alternatives to popular big tech B2B tools. Covers categories including analytics (Plausible vs Google Analytics), email marketing (Brevo vs Mailchimp), cloud hosting (Hetzner vs AWS), team communication (Element vs Slack), AI (Mistral vs ChatGPT), password management (Passbolt vs 1Password), video conferencing (Whereby vs Zoom), and more. Each entry includes country of origin, hosting location, GDPR compliance status, and pricing. Self-hosted open-source alternatives are also noted where applicable.

recent_posts.title: What are backlinks in SEO and how to get them?
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to backlinks in SEO covering what they are, why they matter, and how to evaluate their quality. Explains the difference between dofollow and nofollow links, domain authority metrics from tools like Moz, Ahrefs, and Semrush, and how anchor text affects rankings. Covers both organic and manual link-building strategies including guest posting, broken link building, unlinked brand mentions, and competitor analysis. Also addresses black-hat practices to avoid (buying links, comment spam, excessive link exchanges), how to measure backlink impact using web analytics and SEO tools, and how to conduct backlink audits including using Google's Disavow Tool.

recent_posts.title: Why Plausible Analytics stays bootstrapped and rejects investor funding
recent_posts.summary: Plausible Analytics explains why it has never taken investor funding and remains 100% subscriber-supported. The team argues that staying bootstrapped preserves their privacy-first mission, prevents data monetization pressure, and allows them to stay small and focused. They outline the tradeoffs accepted — slower growth, fewer integrations, no free tier — and why those are worth the independence, calm work culture, and long-term trust they gain in return.

recent_posts.title: How to transition to Plausible after GA4?
recent_posts.summary: A practical migration guide for marketers moving from GA4 to Plausible Analytics. Covers the core philosophical differences (privacy-first vs user profiling), setup steps including GA data import, and side-by-side comparisons for common tasks: traffic overview, campaign/UTM tracking, audience segmentation with custom properties, SEO via Search Console integration, e-commerce revenue tracking, funnel analysis, and custom reporting via Looker Studio or Stats API. Also highlights Plausible-exclusive features like automatic scroll depth tracking, embeddable dashboards, and Slack alerts. Ends with a comparison table noting GA4 advantages (retention/cohorts, multi-touch attribution) that Plausible intentionally omits for privacy reasons.

recent_posts.title: Consent Mode and how GA4 fills missing data with behavioral modeling and modeled conversions
recent_posts.summary: Google Consent Mode is a system that allows GA4 tags to fire even when users reject cookie tracking, sending limited 'cookieless pings' that are combined with behavioral patterns from consenting users to model estimated conversions and sessions. In advanced mode, GA4 mixes real observed data with machine-learning predictions without distinguishing between them in reports, making it impossible to know how much of your dashboard reflects actual user behavior. This creates a legal gray area since data is still sent to Google servers before anonymization, and small sites often can't meet the minimum thresholds required to activate modeling at all. Plausible is presented as a cookieless, privacy-first alternative that collects only real event data without requiring consent banners, behavioral modeling, GTM configuration, or BigQuery exports.

recent_posts.title: Why analytics tools report different numbers and how to interpret the gaps
recent_posts.summary: Analytics tools rarely show identical numbers, and this post explains why. Key factors include cookie consent requirements, ad-blocker and browser script blocking, differing metric definitions (clicks vs visits vs impressions), bot filtering approaches, data modeling vs raw measurement, and implementation issues. The post walks through five comparison categories: Plausible vs other web analytics tools (e.g., GA4), vs search tools (GSC), vs ad platforms, vs email campaign tools, and vs server logs/hosting dashboards. Each category explains the structural reasons for discrepancies. The practical takeaway is to pick one primary analytics tool, use others for complementary context, and focus on trends rather than matching absolute numbers across tools.

recent_posts.title: ChatGPT referral traffic drops but sends more engaged visitors
recent_posts.summary: ChatGPT referral traffic has dropped ~52% industry-wide since July 21, with a sharper decline after GPT-5 launched on August 7. Analysis of Plausible's own dashboard shows visits down 29%, but engagement metrics improved: views per visit up 11%, bounce rate down 3%, visit duration up 16%, and conversion rates slightly higher. The shift appears driven by ChatGPT favoring high-trust, neutral sources like Wikipedia and Reddit. Recommendations for site owners include shifting to answer-first content, building brand and community, refreshing content regularly, and publishing original research or thought leadership that only your brand can provide.
